title: What is known about 1RB0LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RA_0LF1LD_1LC1RF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RA_0LF1LD_1LC1RF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The head shuttles out from the left end over the background word 100110001001, turning back or passing at each defect depending on its shape (so the defects act as the digits of a counter), and rewriting the background as (01)^4 1^4 going right and back going left (proved in Lean). Defects of the background move as gliders from a gun at the left end to a few nearly stationary defects near the right end, which grows in rare bursts. No macro map is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 53,101 cells have been visited and 25,038 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The two sweeps over the background
claims.text: Going right, A crosses (000100110011)^n in 28n steps and leaves (101011111010)^n, a rotation of (01)^4 1^4; going left, D crosses ((01)^4 1^4)^n in 60n steps and leaves a rotation of the background.

claims.title: The right end grows in rare events
claims.text: Up to 3·109 steps the right end grows in 23 bursts (at 4452, 34862, …, 349120206, 601597011, 1209167380, 2298066779, 2605468340); they alternate between two shapes, ending …1100 and …0101100.

claims.title: Bursts and glider births
claims.text: A new glider appears at the left end within one sweep after most bursts of the second shape (e.g. bursts at 62687, 111515, 1680471, 3889033, 44193243, 140427539, 601597011; births at 64571, 114290, 1690591, 3906687, 44244711, 140517476, 601771479), up to 1.3·10<sup>9</sup> steps.

claims.title: Gliders, merges and a pile
claims.text: Gliders move right, then slow down and merge; three or four nearly stationary defects sit within about 300 words of the right end. Around 2·108 steps the head, leaving the left end, turns at the first defect on most excursions and passes it on 3 of every 12 (pattern 000010001010, 1 = passes).

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.484). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.071).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Next step: Catalogue the glider shapes, speeds and merge rules and the two right-end reactions, then accelerate the run as a particle system.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape of this machine is one 12-cell word repeated, with a handful of defects that move like particles: a gun at the left end shoots gliders that slow down, merge and pile up near the right end, which grows only in rare bursts.

facts.text: The head's sweeps over the background, proved for every length.
Bursts of growth at the right end in 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps.
No halt in the C simulator; 53,101 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A 12-cell word in two phases
html: When the head is back at the left end the tape reads 100110001001 over and over; the sweep to the right turns each copy into (01)^4 1^4 (28 steps a word), the sweep to the left turns it back (60 steps a word). Each return of the head to the left end (in state E) adds four cells there, a word every three returns.

sections.heading: Gliders and a pile
html:
The dark lines are defects that every sweep reshapes and moves. They are born at the left end, shortly after a burst of growth at the right end, travel right, slow down and merge, and end in a few almost stationary defects near the right end. Bursts get rarer as the tape grows (23 in 3·109 steps), so the right side grows like a logarithm.

A halt needs B reading 1. Nothing in the run so far comes close, and the collision rules are not known, so there is no estimate either way.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.484). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.071).
After 109 steps the tape spans 53,101 cells (33,407 left of the start, 72 right), with a density of 1s of 0.472.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: Glider collider: a bouncer over a period-12 background, gun at the left end, counter at the right
summary: A bouncer over the period-12 background 100110001001 / (01)^4 1^4 carrying gliders: every second burst at the slow right end makes the left end emit a glider, which drifts right and merges into the pile near the right end.
